nodes.description: The team's non-negotiable design principles — from Figma-as-blueprint to accessibility-first, tokens as contracts, and no placeholders ever.
nodes.body:
# Team Design Convictions

Our non-negotiable design principles. These guide every decision — in Figma, in code, in how we use Claude.

---

## Figma is a blueprint, not a deliverable

Every static frame is a brief for its living counterpart. If a Figma comp does not imply how it moves, it is incomplete. Motion annotations with actual spring constants, ARIA roles, and state descriptions sit in separate annotation frames beside the design — never inside it.

## We never build from scratch what the system already provides

The atomic hierarchy — fundamentals -> components -> blocks -> templates — governs every file. `figma_instantiate_component` is the primary build method. If you find yourself recreating a button or card from raw frames and text nodes, something has gone wrong.

See: [[design-system-patterns]]

## A design with placeholders is not a design

No gray boxes, no Lorem ipsum, no generic icons. Real images, real text copied from the source. We cannot judge hierarchy, visual weight, or emotional tone with placeholders.

## Design tokens are the contract between design and development

We do not guess at colors or round spacing values. If the design says `#216D6A` and 20px padding, the code says `#216D6A` and 20px padding. Every token flows from Figma to CSS custom properties with exact values.

See: [[design-system-patterns]]

## Mobile is not a smaller desktop

It is a different medium — touch, scroll, limited attention, one-handed use. We classify each desktop section as Mode A (simple reflow) or Mode B (pattern rethink). Reflowing is the easy path; rethinking is where the design value lives.

## Accessibility is a design constraint, not a development task

We choose patterns partly based on how well they support keyboard and screen reader use. If we cannot describe the ARIA roles and focus management for an interaction, it is not ready to build.

## Animation is part of the design system

Every motion answers: what changed and why? We pick the animation tool that matches the interaction model. `prefers-reduced-motion` fallback is non-negotiable.

## The screenshot is the source of truth

We extract programmatically via MCP, translate to our stack's conventions, and validate with screenshots. Visual validation is mandatory, with up to 3 iterations.

## Duplication is a design system failure

If a block exists, it gets reused. Every project should have a block reuse matrix mapping blocks across templates.

nodes.body:
# Design System Patterns

Shared patterns for building and maintaining design systems across projects.

---

## Atomic Hierarchy

```
Fundamentals (colors, type, spacing, icons)
  -> Components (button, card, input, tag)
    -> Blocks (hero, carousel section, FAQ accordion, contact CTA)
      -> Templates (page layouts assembled from blocks)
```

See: [[convictions]] — "We never build from scratch what the system already provides"

## Auto-Layout Rules

- Always use auto-layout. No absolute positioning unless overlapping elements require it.
- `layoutSizingHorizontal = "FILL"` on all content containers.
- Set exact values for all properties — never use defaults.
- Name every layer semantically: PascalCase for components (`CarouselTrack`), kebab-case with `--modifier` for states (`AccordionItem--expanded`).

## Typography Scaling (Desktop -> Mobile)

| Level | Desktop | Mobile | Rules |
|-------|---------|--------|-------|
| Headlines | Source size | 60-70% of desktop, min 24px | Line-height 1.15-1.2. Tighten letter-spacing for large display type |
| Subheads | Source size | 65-75%, min 18px | |
| Body | Source size | 15-17px, never below 14px | Line-height 1.4-1.55 |
| Captions | Source size | 12-13px | Line-height 1.3-1.4 |

## Spacing System

| Context | Desktop | Mobile | Rule |
|---------|---------|--------|------|
| Horizontal padding | Project-specific | 20-24px edge inset | Non-negotiable mobile minimum |
| Touch targets | N/A | Min 44px height | Non-negotiable |
| Section gaps | Project-specific | Compress proportionally | Ratio between gaps matters more than absolute values |

## Gestalt Principles

- **Proximity**: Tighten related groups further on mobile. Increase separation between unrelated groups.
- **Similarity**: Identical styling for elements serving the same function.
- **Continuity**: Vertical flow must feel unbroken. Align left edges strictly.
- **Optical centering**: Shift ~2-4% upward from mathematical center for perceived balance.

## Web Implementation Patterns

| Pattern | Lightweight | Rich |
|---------|------------|------|
| Carousel | CSS `scroll-snap-type: x mandatory` | Framer Motion `drag="x"` or Embla Carousel |
| Accordion | `<details>/<summary>` (zero JS) | Framer Motion `AnimatePresence` + `layout` |
| Tabs | `tablist/tab/tabpanel` roles + CSS | Framer Motion `layoutId` for indicator |
| Images | `next/image` with `sizes`, `placeholder="blur"`, `loading="lazy"` | — |

## Project Token Catalogs

Project-specific tokens live in their respective folders:
- [[museon]] — `projects/museon/`
- [[pulse]] — `projects/pulse/`
- [[solara]] — `projects/solara/`

nodes.body:
# Team Workflows

Standard workflows for using Claude + Figma Console MCP across projects.

---

## Figma Console MCP — The Primary Tool

Figma Console MCP is the primary tool for **both** building in Figma and extracting designs for web implementation. It gives direct access to the Figma plugin API — exact computed values, image hashes, every property — which is more precise than the Figma API MCP.

### Building inside Figma (everyone)

The core workflow for the whole team — designing, exploring, and building components and pages in Figma.

| Step | Tool | Purpose |
|------|------|---------|
| 1 | `figma_search_components` | Know what exists before building (run at session start) |
| 2 | `figma_get_selection` | Get selected node structure — layout, hierarchy, properties |
| 3 | `figma_take_screenshot` | Visual reference — the source of truth |
| 4 | `figma_get_component_details` | Inspect component properties, variants, states |
| 5 | `figma_get_styles` | Extract exact colors, typography, spacing tokens |
| 6 | `figma_instantiate_component` | Build with existing components — primary method |
| 7 | `figma_clone_node` / `figma_set_image_fill` | Transfer real images |
| 8 | `figma_execute` | Custom operations, complex builds, batch variable creation |
| 9 | `figma_take_screenshot` | Validate, iterate up to 3x |

See: [[convictions]] — "We never build from scratch what the system already provides"

### Extracting for web implementation

Workflow for translating Figma designs to code. Uses the same Console MCP tools for reading, plus the API MCP for quick URL-based extraction.

| Step | Tool | Purpose |
|------|------|---------|
| 1 | `figma_get_selection` + `figma_take_screenshot` | Understand the design visually and structurally |
| 2 | `figma_get_component_details` + `figma_get_styles` | Extract exact tokens, props, variants |
| 3 | `figma_execute` | Custom extraction — image hashes, computed values, anything the plugin API exposes |
| 4 | Translate to project conventions | Map tokens to CSS custom properties, reuse existing code components |
| 5 | Validate against screenshot | Layout, typography, colors, states, accessibility |

### Figma API MCP (secondary)

The Figma API MCP (`get_design_context`, `get_screenshot`, `get_metadata`) is useful when:
- Figma Desktop is not open (works via URL only)
- You need a quick one-shot extraction from a shared link
- You want Code Connect mappings between Figma components and codebase files

**Key insight:** Extracting Figma **components** (not raw frames) via `get_design_context` produces richer output — typed as `COMPONENT`/`INSTANCE`, exposes props/variants.

## Figma Build Order (for `figma_execute`)

1. Create the node (frame, text, rectangle)
2. For text: set `fontName` BEFORE `characters`
3. Load ALL fonts with `figma.loadFontAsync()` at start — including `Inter Regular` (Figma default)
4. Append node to parent BEFORE setting `layoutSizingHorizontal = "FILL"` (requires auto-layout parent)
5. For hug-content containers: set `primaryAxisSizingMode = "AUTO"` AFTER appending children

## Visual Validation Loop

After creating or modifying ANY visual elements:
1. **CREATE**: Execute design code via `figma_execute`
2. **SCREENSHOT**: Capture result with `figma_take_screenshot`
3. **ANALYZE**: Check alignment, spacing, proportions, visual balance
4. **ITERATE**: Fix issues and repeat (max 3 iterations)
5. **VERIFY**: Final screenshot to confirm

## Desktop-to-Mobile Translation

1. **Analyze** — `figma_get_selection` + `figma_take_screenshot` + `figma_get_component_details` + `figma_get_styles`
2. **Classify each section** as Mode A (simple reflow) or Mode B (pattern rethink)
3. **Mode A** — Build reflow directly, no approval needed
4. **Mode B** — Present pattern proposals with motion specs, wait for approval
5. **Build** — 375px frame, auto-layout, component-first, real images, exact tokens
6. **Annotate** — Motion/interaction specs in separate frame beside the design (40px gap)
7. **Validate** — Screenshot, analyze, fix, re-screenshot (up to 3 iterations)

## Divergent Exploration

See: [[diverge]] — full skill for generating 3 design directions as Figma frames.

# Mobile UX Pattern Advisor

  

You are a senior UX designer and front-end architect. You combine deep interaction design knowledge with practical web development experience — you know what works beautifully on mobile AND what ships cleanly in HTML/CSS/JS.

  

Your task: analyze the selected desktop design block(s), identify UX opportunities for mobile, propose interaction patterns, and — once the user approves a direction — build it in Figma using the Figma Console MCP.

  

This skill is NOT a pixel-for-pixel translator. It is a **design thinker** that reimagines how content should behave on a small, touch-driven, scroll-driven screen — while staying faithful to the visual identity.

  

---

  

## STACK CONTEXT

  

The user works in a pipeline: **Figma → Next.js (React)**.

  

- **Design system**: Atomic design — fundamentals → components → blocks → templates.

- **Frontend**: Next.js with React for CSS, Framer Motion for animation.

- **Tooling**: Claude Code with Pierre, Figma MCP for implementation, Figma Console MCP for extraction from Figma, Blender MCP.

- **Key insight**: Figma is static, but the final product is not. When proposing patterns, think beyond what Figma can show — describe the **motion, timing, and interaction states** that will come alive in code. Design in Figma as a blueprint for a living interface, not as a final artifact.

  

When annotating designs, include Framer Motion thinking: what animates, how, and when. This bridges the gap between the static Figma comp and the dynamic Next.js implementation.

  

---

  

## WORKFLOW

  

### Phase 1 — Deep Analysis

  

1. **Get the current selection** via `figma_get_selection`.

2. **Take a screenshot** via `figma_take_screenshot` to see the full composition.

3. **Inspect thoroughly** via `figma_get_component_details` and `figma_get_styles`:

- Map every element: text, images, icons, buttons, links, containers.

- Identify the **content type** of each section (see Content Pattern Library below).

- Note data density: how many items? How repetitive? How much text per item?

- Identify interactive elements vs. static content.

- Extract all visual tokens (colors, type, spacing, radii) for later use.

- Identify which elements are **fundamentals**, **components**, or **blocks** in the atomic hierarchy — this affects how the mobile pattern should decompose.

4. **Search for components** via `figma_search_components` to understand the design system and reuse existing atoms.

  

### Phase 2 — UX Pattern Mapping

  

For each section/block in the selection, classify its **content archetype** and evaluate which mobile interaction patterns fit. Consider:

  

#### Content Archetypes → Pattern Candidates

  

| Content Type | Desktop Appearance | Mobile Pattern Options |

|---|---|---|

| **Item collection** (events, products, articles, cards) | Grid of 3-4+ cards | **Horizontal carousel** (peek next item to invite swipe), **Vertical stack** (if ≤3 items), **2-col compact grid** (if items are image-heavy and small) |

| **Feature list** (services, benefits, steps) | Multi-column icons + text | **Vertical accordion** (if descriptions are long), **Swipeable cards** (if visual), **Simple stack** (if concise) |

| **Navigation / categories** | Horizontal row or mega-menu | **Scrollable pill tabs**, **Bottom sheet with categories**, **Segmented control** (if ≤4 items) |

| **Hero / banner** | Full-width with text overlay | **Stacked: image then text** (safer for readability), **Compact hero** (shorter image, overlapping text card) |

| **Testimonials / quotes** | Side-by-side or grid | **Carousel with dots/pagination**, **Single featured + "see more"** |

| **Stats / numbers** | Horizontal row | **2x2 grid**, **Horizontal scroll**, **Single stat highlight + expandable** |

| **Long-form text** | Wide paragraphs | **Progressive disclosure** (show first paragraph + "Read more"), **Accordion sections** if content has natural divisions |

| **Media gallery** | Grid of images | **Full-width carousel with counter**, **Masonry 2-col** (if varied aspect ratios), **Horizontal filmstrip** |

| **Form / input** | Wide multi-column form | **Single-column stepped form**, **Floating labels**, **Bottom-anchored CTA** |

| **Tab content** | Horizontal tabs with content panels | **Sticky tabs** (remain visible on scroll), **Swipeable tab content** |

| **Map + list** | Side-by-side | **Toggle view** (map/list switch), **Bottom sheet over map** |

nodes.description: Redesigns the Museon collection block from a flat carousel into an editorial hybrid layout that preserves the art-catalogue feel on mobile.
nodes.body:
# Mobile Collection Block — Editorial Hybrid Redesign

## Context

The desktop "View our highlights" collection block has a striking editorial layout: three artworks at different sizes, asymmetrically placed — like an art catalogue spread. The current mobile version flattens this into a generic equal-width horizontal carousel, losing the editorial character.

**Goal**: Redesign as a **hybrid layout** — one large hero artwork on top, followed by a peek-style carousel for the remaining pieces. Then implement in Next.js/React code.

---

## Phase A — Build in Figma

### Steps

1. **Create Section** on current page: `Mobile UX — Collection Editorial Hybrid`
2. **Build mobile frame** (375px wide, auto-layout vertical, bg `#216D6A`, padding 20px horizontal / 60px vertical, 80px gap between major sections)
3. **Title block** — "View our highlights" at 40px Display Sans `#FFE176`, ornament below
4. **Hero artwork** — Full-width image container (fills parent width). Use the landscape painting. Below it: title + artist in `#FFE176`
5. **Carousel section** — Horizontal auto-layout, overflow hidden:
   - Card 1: ~280px wide (Guest Architect illustration)
   - Card 2: ~20% peeking (third artwork)
   - 16px gap between cards
6. **Pagination row** — "2 / 3" counter + dot indicators
7. **Info section** — Body text + "View collection" CTA with arrow
8. **Decorative ornaments** — Scatter between sections
9. **Annotation frame** beside the design with motion specs + component mapping
10. **Screenshot & validate** — Check hierarchy, peek visibility, proportions. Iterate up to 3x.

### Visual tokens
- Background: `#216D6A`
- Title: `#FFE176`, Display Sans Regular 40px, lh 1.1, tracking -0.8px
- Body/labels: `#FFE176`, Display Sans Regular 16px, lh 1.4
- Artist: `#FFE176`, Display Sans Regular 12px, lh 1.4
- Accent: `#A6E3E6`
- Padding: 20px horizontal, 60px vertical
- Gaps: 80px between sections, 20px image-to-text

### Key Figma nodes
- Current mobile: `6177:3097`
- Desktop: `6099:2869`
- Component set: `6099:2881`
- Decoration: Contemporary Artist ornament variants
- CTA pattern: `6176:3091`
- DotsGroup: `6176:3085`

---

## Phase B — Implement in Code (Next.js / React)

### Component structure

```
CollectionSectionBlock (mobile variant)
├── Title ("View our highlights")
├── Decoration (ornament)
├── HeroArtwork
│   ├── Image (next/image, full-width, natural aspect ratio)
│   └── Details (title + artist)
├── CarouselSection
│   ├── CarouselTrack (horizontal scroll-snap)
│   │   ├── CarouselCard (remaining item 1)
│   │   └── CarouselCard (remaining item 2, peeking)
│   └── PaginationRow (counter + dots)
├── InfoSection
│   ├── BodyText
│   └── CTAButton ("View collection" →)
└── Decoration (ornament)
```

### Implementation approach

- **Hero**: `next/image` with `sizes="100vw"`, `placeholder="blur"`, fills container width, natural aspect ratio
- **Carousel**: CSS `scroll-snap-type: x mandatory` + `overflow-x: auto` on the track. Cards with `scroll-snap-align: start`. Peek achieved by making track wider than viewport with right padding.
- **Pagination**: Intersection Observer on carousel cards to update active index + counter text
- **Styling**: React CSS (styled-jsx or CSS modules, matching project conventions)
- **Motion (Framer Motion)**:
  - Hero: `whileInView` fade-up, `y: [30,0]`, `opacity: [0,1]`, `duration: 0.6`
  - Hero text: 0.1s delay after image
  - Carousel cards: slide in from right on first view, `x: [60,0]`
  - Card swipe: spring snap (`stiffness: 300, damping: 30`)
  - Ornaments: gentle scroll-driven rotation
  - `prefers-reduced-motion`: all visible, no animation

### Files to create/modify
- Determine from existing codebase — search for existing collection block component and mobile variant patterns

---

## Verification

### Figma
1. Screenshot confirms hero is clearly larger/dominant
2. Carousel shows peek of next card
3. All real images, no placeholders
4. Annotations beside (not overlapping) the design
5. All layers named semantically (PascalCase)

### Code
1. Component renders correctly at 375px viewport
2. Carousel scrolls horizontally with snap
3. Peek visible on next card
4. Hero image loads with proper sizing
5. Framer Motion animations fire on scroll
6. CTA touch target ≥ 44px
7. `prefers-reduced-motion` respected

# Desktop to Mobile — Unified Translation

You are a world-class visual designer and front-end architect with deep knowledge of Gestalt principles, optical correction, and mobile interaction patterns — in the tradition of Max Bill's systematic precision and visual clarity.

Your task: translate the desktop design blocks I provide into mobile-optimized versions inside Figma, using the Figma Console MCP. Depending on the content, you will either **faithfully reflow** the layout or **propose a new interaction pattern** — you decide which approach fits, section by section.

---

## STACK CONTEXT

The user works in a pipeline: **Figma → Next.js (React)**.

- **Design system**: Atomic design — fundamentals → components → blocks → templates.
- **Frontend**: Next.js with React for CSS, Framer Motion for animation.
- **Tooling**: Claude Code with Pierre, Figma MCP for implementation, Figma Console MCP for extraction from Figma, Blender MCP.
- **Key insight**: Figma is static, but the final product is not. When proposing patterns, think beyond what Figma can show — describe the **motion, timing, and interaction states** that will come alive in code. Design in Figma as a blueprint for a living interface, not as a final artifact.

---

## WORKFLOW

### Phase 1 — Analyze the Input

1. **Get the current selection** via `figma_get_selection`.
2. **Take a screenshot** via `figma_take_screenshot` to see the full composition.
3. **Inspect thoroughly** via `figma_get_component_details` and `figma_get_styles`:
   - Extract every color, typeface, font size, weight, line-height, letter-spacing.
   - Extract every spacing value (padding, margin, gap).
   - Extract corner radii, stroke weights, opacity values.
   - Identify all components, instances, auto-layout settings, and constraints.
   - Note the visual hierarchy: what leads the eye, what is primary/secondary/tertiary.
   - Identify which elements are **fundamentals**, **components**, or **blocks** in the atomic hierarchy.
   - Note data density: how many items? How repetitive? How much text per item?
   - Identify interactive elements vs. static content.
4. **Search for components** via `figma_search_components` to understand the design system and reuse existing atoms.

### Phase 2 — Classify Each Section

For each section/block in the selection, determine the **translation mode**:

#### Mode A — Simple Reflow

Use when the content adapts naturally to a single column without losing meaning or usability. Typical candidates:
- Hero / banner (image + headline + CTA)
- Text sections (heading + paragraphs)
- Single feature highlight (image + text side-by-side → stacked)
- Simple navigation (≤5 items)
- Contact / footer blocks
- Any section with ≤3 items that can stack vertically without excessive scroll depth

**Action**: Apply reflow directly using the design rules below. No approval needed — just build.

#### Mode B — Pattern Rethink

Use when a simple reflow would create problems — excessive scroll depth, lost context, broken relationships between items, or missed interaction opportunities. Typical candidates:
- Item collections (grids of 4+ cards — events, products, articles)
- Feature lists (multi-column icons + descriptions)
- Media galleries (image grids)
- Comparison tables / pricing
- Tab content / segmented views
- Timelines / multi-step processes
- Stats / number rows (4+ items)
- Any section where vertical stacking creates a wall of repetitive content

**Action**: Propose pattern options, wait for approval, then build.

Present Mode B sections to the user:

```

**Content type**: [archetype]
**Atomic level**: [fundamental / component / block]
**Desktop**: [brief description of current layout]
**Items/data points**: [count and nature]

**Recommended pattern**: [Pattern A]
- Why: [UX rationale]
- Motion: [Framer Motion behavior — enter, interact, exit]
- Implementation: [Next.js/React approach, complexity level]

**Alternative**: [Pattern B]
- Why: [when this would be better instead]

**What stays the same**: [visual identity elements preserved]
**What becomes possible**: [motion, gesture, state — things code enables beyond static]
```

After presenting Mode B proposals, **ask the user which direction to take**. Proceed with Mode A sections immediately while waiting.

| Content Type | Desktop Appearance | Mobile Pattern Options |

| **Item collection** (events, products, articles, cards) | Grid of 3-4+ cards | **Horizontal carousel** (peek next item to invite swipe), **Vertical stack** (if ≤3 items), **2-col compact grid** (if image-heavy and small) |
| **Feature list** (services, benefits, steps) | Multi-column icons + text | **Vertical accordion** (if descriptions are long), **Swipeable cards** (if visual), **Simple stack** (if concise) |

nodes.body:
# Figma MCP: Frame vs. Component — Cosa cambia nell'estrazione web

## Contesto
Quando usi il **Figma MCP** (`get_design_context`) per portare un design sul web, il tipo di nodo che selezioni influenza la qualità e l'utilità del codice generato.

---

## Frame semplice

Quando chiami `get_design_context` su un frame normale, il MCP lo tratta come uno **snapshot statico** di quel nodo specifico:

- Restituisce layout, stili e struttura dei layer figli
- Genera codice per quell'istanza esatta
- **Nessun segnale di riusabilità** — il MCP non sa che quel design è pensato per essere usato in più posti

---

## Componente (o istanza di componente)

Quando il frame è un **componente Figma**, il MCP riceve metadati più ricchi:

- Il nodo è tipizzato come `COMPONENT` o `INSTANCE` (non solo `FRAME`), segnalando chiaramente l'intento di riusabilità
- Le **component properties** (varianti, prop booleane, override di testo) vengono esposte → il codice generato può riflettere cose come `size="lg"` o `disabled={true}` invece di valori hardcoded
- Si può usare **Code Connect** — questo è il punto chiave: puoi collegare il componente Figma a un file reale nel tuo codebase (`Button.tsx`, ecc.), così `get_design_context` restituisce *il tuo* componente esistente invece di rigenerare codice da zero

---

## Confronto pratico

|  | Frame semplice | Componente |
|---|---|---|
| Codice generato | HTML/CSS/JSX letterale che replica i layer | Stesso, ma può mappare al tuo codebase reale via Code Connect |
| Props/varianti esposte | ❌ | ✅ |
| Segnale di riusabilità | Nessuno | Forte |
| Code Connect compatibile | ❌ | ✅ |
| Istanze multiple sincronizzate | N/A | Tutte le istanze condividono la stessa definizione |

---

## Quando fa davvero la differenza

**Non cambia molto** se vuoi solo una traduzione una-tantum di un design statico in codice web — il MCP genera codice ragionevole in entrambi i casi.

**Fa molta differenza** se:
- Il frame viene riusato in più punti (nav, card, button, ecc.)
- Vuoi che il codice generato rifletta **props/varianti** invece di valori hardcoded
- Hai impostato (o vuoi impostare) **Code Connect** per puntare il MCP al tuo codebase esistente invece di rigenerare codice ogni volta

---

## Regola pratica

> **Fallo diventare un componente se è pensato per essere riusabile.** Il MCP produrrà codice molto più utile, guidato da props, e potrà agganciarsi alla tua component library reale.

Prerequisites
Figma MCP server must be connected and accessible
Before proceeding, verify the Figma MCP server is connected by checking if Figma MCP tools (e.g., get_design_context) are available.
If the tools are not available, the Figma MCP server may not be enabled. Guide the user to enable the Figma MCP server that is included with the plugin. They may need to restart their MCP client afterward.
User must provide a Figma URL in the format: https://figma.com/design/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=1-2
:fileKey is the file key
1-2 is the node ID (the specific component or frame to implement)
Project should have an established design system or component library (preferred)
Required Workflow
Follow these steps in order. Do not skip steps.

Step 1: Get Node ID
Option A: Parse from Figma URL
When the user provides a Figma URL, extract the file key and node ID to pass as arguments to MCP tools.

URL format: https://figma.com/design/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=1-2

Extract:

File key: :fileKey (the segment after /design/)
Node ID: 1-2 (the value of the node-id query parameter)
Example:

URL: https://figma.com/design/tU5vW6xY7zA8bC9dE0fG1h/DesignSystem?node-id=42-15
File key: tU5vW6xY7zA8bC9dE0fG1h
Node ID: 42-15
Step 2: Fetch Design Context
Run get_design_context with the extracted file key and node ID.

get_design_context(fileKey=":fileKey", nodeId="1-2")

This provides the structured data including:

Layout properties (Auto Layout, constraints, sizing)
Typography specifications
Color values and design tokens
Component structure and variants
Spacing and padding values
If the response is too large or truncated:

Run get_metadata(fileKey=":fileKey", nodeId="1-2") to get the high-level node map
Identify the specific child nodes needed from the metadata
Fetch individual child nodes with get_design_context(fileKey=":fileKey", nodeId=":childNodeId")
Step 3: Capture Visual Reference
Run get_screenshot with the same file key and node ID for a visual reference.

get_screenshot(fileKey=":fileKey", nodeId="1-2")

This screenshot serves as the source of truth for visual validation. Keep it accessible throughout implementation.

Step 4: Download Required Assets
Download any assets (images, icons, SVGs) returned by the Figma MCP server.

IMPORTANT: Follow these asset rules:

If the Figma MCP server returns a localhost source for an image or SVG, use that source directly
DO NOT import or add new icon packages - all assets should come from the Figma payload
DO NOT use or create placeholders if a localhost source is provided
Assets are served through the Figma MCP server's built-in assets endpoint
Step 5: Translate to Project Conventions
Translate the Figma output into this project's framework, styles, and conventions.

Key principles:

Treat the Figma MCP output (typically React + Tailwind) as a representation of design and behavior, not as final code style
Replace Tailwind utility classes with the project's preferred utilities or design system tokens
Reuse existing components (buttons, inputs, typography, icon wrappers) instead of duplicating functionality
Use the project's color system, typography scale, and spacing tokens consistently
Respect existing routing, state management, and data-fetch patterns
Step 6: Achieve 1:1 Visual Parity
Strive for pixel-perfect visual parity with the Figma design.

Guidelines:

Prioritize Figma fidelity to match designs exactly
Avoid hardcoded values - use design tokens from Figma where available
When conflicts arise between design system tokens and Figma specs, prefer design system tokens but adjust spacing or sizes minimally to match visuals
Follow WCAG requirements for accessibility
Add component documentation as needed
Step 7: Validate Against Figma
Before marking complete, validate the final UI against the Figma screenshot.

Validation checklist:

 Layout matches (spacing, alignment, sizing)
 Typography matches (font, size, weight, line height)
 Colors match exactly
 Interactive states work as designed (hover, active, disabled)
 Responsive behavior follows Figma constraints
 Assets render correctly
 Accessibility standards met
Implementation Rules
Component Organization
Place UI components in the project's designated design system directory
Follow the project's component naming conventions
Avoid inline styles unless truly necessary for dynamic values
Design System Integration
ALWAYS use components from the project's design system when possible
Map Figma design tokens to project design tokens
When a matching component exists, extend it rather than creating a new one
Document any new components added to the design system
Code Quality
Avoid hardcoded values - extract to constants or design tokens
Keep components composable and reusable
Add TypeScript types for component props
Include JSDoc comments for exported components

# Implement Design from Figma

Translate the provided Figma design into production-ready code with 1:1 visual parity.

## Prerequisites

- Figma MCP server must be connected and accessible
- Verify by checking if Figma MCP tools (e.g., `get_design_context`) are available
- If tools are unavailable, guide the user to enable the Figma MCP server and restart their MCP client

## Required Workflow

Follow these steps in order. Do not skip steps.

### Step 1: Parse the Figma URL

Extract the file key and node ID from the provided URL: `$ARGUMENTS.url`

URL format: `https://figma.com/design/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=1-2`

- **File key**: the segment after `/design/`
- **Node ID**: the value of the `node-id` query parameter (convert `-` to `:` as needed)
- For branch URLs (`/design/:fileKey/branch/:branchKey/...`), use `branchKey` as the file key

### Step 2: Fetch Design Context

Run `get_design_context` with the extracted file key and node ID.

This provides:
- Layout properties (Auto Layout, constraints, sizing)
- Typography specifications
- Color values and design tokens
- Component structure and variants
- Spacing and padding values

If the response is too large or truncated:
1. Run `get_metadata` to get the high-level node map
2. Identify specific child nodes from the metadata
3. Fetch individual child nodes with `get_design_context`

### Step 3: Capture Visual Reference

Run `get_screenshot` with the same file key and node ID. This screenshot is the source of truth for visual validation throughout implementation.

### Step 4: Download Required Assets

Download any assets (images, icons, SVGs) returned by the Figma MCP server.

**Asset rules:**
- If a localhost source is returned for an image or SVG, use that source directly
- DO NOT import or add new icon packages — all assets should come from the Figma payload
- DO NOT use or create placeholders if a localhost source is provided
- Assets are served through the Figma MCP server's built-in assets endpoint

### Step 5: Translate to Project Conventions

Translate the Figma output into this project's framework, styles, and conventions:

- Treat the Figma MCP output (typically React + Tailwind) as a representation of design and behavior, not final code
- Replace Tailwind utility classes with the project's preferred utilities or design system tokens
- Reuse existing components (buttons, inputs, typography, icon wrappers) instead of duplicating
- Use the project's color system, typography scale, and spacing tokens consistently
- Respect existing routing, state management, and data-fetch patterns

### Step 6: Achieve 1:1 Visual Parity

- Prioritize Figma fidelity to match designs exactly
- Avoid hardcoded values — use design tokens from Figma where available
- When conflicts arise between design system tokens and Figma specs, prefer design system tokens but adjust spacing/sizes minimally to match visuals
- Follow WCAG requirements for accessibility

### Step 7: Validate Against Figma

Before marking complete, validate the final UI against the Figma screenshot.

**Validation checklist:**
- [ ] Layout matches (spacing, alignment, sizing)
- [ ] Typography matches (font, size, weight, line height)
- [ ] Colors match exactly
- [ ] Interactive states work as designed (hover, active, disabled)
- [ ] Responsive behavior follows Figma constraints
- [ ] Assets render correctly
- [ ] Accessibility standards met

## Implementation Rules

### Component Organization
- Place UI components in the project's designated design system directory
- Follow the project's component naming conventions
- Avoid inline styles unless truly necessary for dynamic values

### Design System Integration
- ALWAYS use components from the project's design system when possible
- Map Figma design tokens to project design tokens
- When a matching component exists, extend it rather than creating a new one

### Code Quality
- Avoid hardcoded values — extract to constants or design tokens
- Keep components composable and reusable
- Add TypeScript types for component props

## Troubleshooting

- **Truncated output**: Use `get_metadata` first, then fetch specific child nodes individually
- **Visual mismatch**: Compare side-by-side with the Step 3 screenshot; check spacing, colors, and typography values
- **Assets not loading**: Verify the Figma MCP server's assets endpoint is accessible; use localhost URLs directly without modification
- **Token value conflicts**: Prefer project tokens for consistency but adjust spacing/sizing to maintain visual fidelity

# sitemap-update-workflow


# Solara — Sitemap Update Workflow

> The Sitemap v2 page in **Solara System Gus** is the atomic source of truth for the design system.
> It is maintained manually via Claude (Option 2) — triggered at the end of any session where components, blocks, or fundamentals change.

---

## When to trigger an update

Trigger this workflow whenever any of the following happen:

- A new **component** is added or renamed (e.g. new button variant, new card type)
- A **block** is created, restructured, or its component composition changes
- A **fundamental** token is added, renamed, or reassigned (type scale, colour, spacing)
- A **template** is added or renamed
- A **page** is added to or removed from the sitemap

Just say: **"update the sitemap"** — Claude will do the rest.

---

## What Claude does on update

1. **Re-reads all Blocks** (desktop components on the Blocks page) using `figma_execute` + `getMainComponentAsync` to detect which components each block uses
2. **Re-reads the Fundamentals pages** (Text, Colours, Spacing, Radius, Elevation) to check for new or renamed tokens
3. **Re-reads the Components pages** to detect new component sets
4. **Diffs** against the current `blockAtoms` data hardcoded in the last sitemap build
5. **Rebuilds the Sitemap v2 canvas** from scratch with updated chip data — legend, hierarchy, all cards
6. **Screenshots** Home card + one item page card to validate visually
